steps.title: Import React, useState, and useEffect
steps.instruction: Import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the hooks you'll need. Remember to destructure useState and useEffect from the React library.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing multiple items from a library
import React, { Component, Fragment } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary React imports are added to enable component creation with state management and side effects
successCriteria: React, useState, and useEffect are imported from 'react'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've imported all the necessary React tools for building components with state and side effects.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you've imported React, useState, and useEffect all in one import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to import React along with the useState and useEffect hooks from the 'react' library.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named EffectDemo
steps.hint: A functional component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX. You can use either function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.seedCode:
// Add your imports here

// Create your EffectDemo component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named EffectDemo is created
successCriteria: EffectDemo component is created as a function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the EffectDemo component. This will be our main component for demonstrating useEffect.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your component is named EffectDemo exactly.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create a functional component named EffectDemo. You can use either function declaration or arrow function syntax.

steps.title: Initialize counter state
steps.instruction: Inside your EffectDemo component, add a count state variable initialized to 0 using useState.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with 0 as the initial value. Remember to destructure both the state variable and its setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating state for a name
const [name, setName] = useState('John');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a count state variable that starts at 0, managed by useState.
successCriteria: A count state variable is created using useState and initialized to 0, with both the state variable and setter function properly destructured.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully created a count state variable using useState. The state is initialized to 0 and you have both the count value and setCount function available.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're using useState with 0 as the initial value and destructuring both the state variable and its setter function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to use the useState hook to create state. You need to destructure both the state variable (count) and its setter function (setCount) from useState(0).

steps.title: Add basic useEffect with console log
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook that logs 'Component rendered' to the console. Place it after the count state initialization.
steps.hint: useEffect takes a function as its first argument. Inside that function, use console.log() to output the message.
steps.expectedOutcome: A useEffect hook is added that will log 'Component rendered' to the console every time the component renders
successCriteria: useEffect is called with a function that contains console.log('Component rendered')
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've added your first useEffect. This will run after every render of the component.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your useEffect contains console.log('Component rendered') with the exact message.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to use useEffect() with a function that contains console.log('Component rendered').

steps.title: Create increment handler function
steps.instruction: Create a function named increment that increases the count state by 1 using setCount.
steps.hint: Use setCount to update the count state. You can pass count + 1 to increment by one.
steps.expectedOutcome: An increment function is defined that updates the count state by adding 1
successCriteria: A function named increment is created that uses setCount to increase count by 1
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created an increment function that will update the count state when called.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your function uses setCount to increase the count by 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment function should use setCount(count + 1) to increase the count state by 1.

steps.title: Create increment handler function
steps.instruction: Create a function named handleIncrement that increments the count state by 1.
steps.hint: Define a function that calls setCount with the current count plus 1. You can use setCount(count + 1) or the callback pattern setCount(prev => prev + 1).
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleIncrement function that updates the count state when called
successCriteria: handleIncrement function is defined and calls setCount to increment the count value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created the increment handler function that will update the count state.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your function calls setCount to increment the count value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment function should call setCount with count + 1 or use the callback pattern setCount(prev => prev + 1).

steps.title: Display the counter value
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element below the heading that displays the current count value using the count state variable.
steps.hint: Use JSX curly braces to display the count variable inside a paragraph element.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: displaying a variable in JSX

Score: {score}
steps.expectedOutcome: The counter value is displayed in a paragraph element below the heading.
successCriteria: A paragraph element displays the count state variable using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully displayed the counter value in the UI. The paragraph shows the current count using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're displaying the count variable inside a paragraph element using curly braces {}.
steps.feedbackWrong: Not quite right. You need to add a paragraph element that displays the count variable using JSX curly braces like {count}.

steps.title: Add increment button with click handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element below the paragraph that displays 'Increment' and calls the increment function when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the button element with onClick event handler to connect user clicks to the increment function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Button that calls a function when clicked
<button onClick={handleSave}>Save</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Increment' appears below the counter display that will trigger the increment function when clicked.
successCriteria: Button element is added with 'Increment' text and onClick handler that calls the increment function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully added an increment button with the onClick handler. Now users can interact with your counter.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your button has the 'Increment' text and the onClick handler calls the increment function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button needs to have 'Increment' as the display text and onClick={increment} to connect to your increment function.

steps.title: Add useEffect with dependency array
steps.instruction: Add a second useEffect that logs 'Count changed to: [count value]' and includes the count variable in its dependency array
steps.hint: Use useEffect with a dependency array [count] as the second parameter to make the effect only run when count changes
steps.expectedOutcome: A second useEffect is added that logs count changes and only runs when the count state changes
successCriteria: Second useEffect with dependency array [count] that logs count value is added
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've added a useEffect with a dependency array. This effect will only run when the count value changes, not on every render.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your useEffect includes the dependency array [count] and logs the count value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect needs a dependency array [count] as the second parameter to control when it runs. Also make sure it logs the count value.

steps.title: Initialize timer state
steps.instruction: Add a second state variable called timer initialized to 0 using useState
steps.hint: Use useState(0) to create the timer state variable, similar to how count was initialized
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating another state variable
const [score, setScore] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: A timer state variable is added to track seconds elapsed
successCriteria: Timer state is initialized to 0 using useState with proper destructuring
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've added a timer state variable that will track elapsed time.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure to use useState(0) and destructure both timer and setTimer.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to add a new state variable using useState(0) with proper destructuring for both the state value and setter function.

steps.title: Add useEffect with setInterval for timer
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook that uses setInterval to increment the timer state by 1 every second (1000 milliseconds).
steps.hint: Use useEffect with setInterval inside it. Call setInterval with a function that increments timer and pass 1000 as the interval duration.
steps.expectedOutcome: A useEffect hook is added that creates a setInterval to increment the timer state every second.
successCriteria: useEffect hook is added with setInterval that increments timer state every 1000 milliseconds
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created a useEffect with setInterval that will increment the timer every second. This demonstrates using useEffect for side effects like timers.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your useEffect uses setInterval to increment the timer state every 1000 milliseconds.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to use useEffect with setInterval inside it. The setInterval should call a function that increments the timer state and run every 1000 milliseconds.

steps.title: Add cleanup function to prevent memory leaks
steps.instruction: Return a cleanup function from the timer useEffect to clear the interval and prevent memory leaks
steps.hint: Return a function from the useEffect that calls clearInterval with the interval ID. This cleanup function will run when the component unmounts or before the effect runs again.
steps.expectedOutcome: The timer useEffect now includes a cleanup function that clears the interval to prevent memory leaks when the component unmounts
successCriteria: The timer useEffect returns a cleanup function that calls clearInterval with the interval variable
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've added a cleanup function that prevents memory leaks by clearing the interval when the component unmounts. This is essential for side effects like timers.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're returning a function from the useEffect that calls clearInterval with the interval variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: Not quite right. You need to return a cleanup function from the useEffect that calls clearInterval(interval) to prevent memory leaks.
